120.title: Five blessings of walking
120.hook: stamina for travel, for effort, good health, good digestion, lasting concentration
120.howItsDone: Many Buddhist monastics and lay practitioners do walking meditation daily, often after meals, and teachers cite the five benefits from the Anguttara Nikaya's walking discourse.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the turn: standing, intending, turning. Your line was the turn counts too. Which in-between moment did you catch? Day one hundred and twenty.

Some families have a tradition: after the big dinner, everyone goes for a slow walk around the block. Nobody calls it medicine. It's just what you do. You feel better, your stomach settles, the conversation gets easier. It turns out the Buddha had his own list of reasons to walk, and one of them would make a grandmother nod. There's a short discourse in the Anguttara Nikaya, the numbered collection, in the book of fives. It lists five blessings of walking meditation. And they're wonderfully practical.
screen: `A SLOW WALK AFTER DINNER.` → `NOBODY CALLS IT MEDICINE.` → `FIVE BLESSINGS OF WALKING.`

segments.voice: The discourse is called the Cankama Sutta, the walking discourse, AN 5.29. Here are the five. One: you can endure long journeys. Remember, the Buddha and his monks walked everywhere, for decades, across northern India. Walking practice helped build the stamina for it. Two: you can endure striving. The effort of practice, the long hours of sitting, the steady work of the path, all come easier to a body used to walking. Three: you're healthy. Four: what you eat and drink is well digested. That's the one the grandmother likes. Five: the concentration you gain while walking lasts a long time. That last one is the most interesting. The discourse simply says it lasts a long time. One way many teachers explain it: concentration built while sitting perfectly still can scatter the moment you stand up. But concentration built while moving, feet lifting, placing, the body turning, is already used to movement, so it may hold up better when you get on with your day. Notice what this list is. It's not mystical. There are no gods, no miracles. It's a teacher telling his students, in plain terms: this is good for your body, good for your practice, and good for the rest of your life. The Pali texts speak about the body in more than one way; elsewhere they ask monks to reflect on its impermanence and unattractiveness. But here, it isn't something to escape or despise. It's the vehicle for the path, and walking keeps it in working order. Today's practice fits the fourth blessing exactly: a slow walk after a meal. Not for steps on a tracker. Just to let the body settle. Walking steadies.
screen: `STAMINA FOR THE ROAD.` · `STAMINA FOR THE EFFORT.` · `HEALTH, AND GOOD DIGESTION.` · `CONCENTRATION THAT LASTS.` · then, large: `WALKING STEADIES.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and walk slowly on your few paces of floor. Feel the whole body walking: the feet, the legs, the belly, the breath. Let the pace be relaxed, a little slower than normal. There's no labeling today unless you want it. Just walking, with attention, as if you'd just finished a good meal and had nowhere to be. At each turn, stand for a breath. If you're seated, feel the body breathing and the feet on the floor. The bell holds the time.
Five blessings of walking. Stamina for the road and for effort, health, good digestion, and concentration that lasts.
Your line: walking steadies. Today, after one meal, take a slow walk, even five minutes, and feel the body settle. Day one hundred and twenty.

pairs: food and drink are well digested

its five blessings are practical: stamina, health, digestion, lasting concentration.
good digestion is one of the five blessings
what you eat and drink is well digested: the fourth.
concentration built while walking holds up well when you move
the fifth blessing: it lasts a long time.

fork.setup: you've just finished a big meal. what does the walking discourse suggest?
options: sit very still for an hour.
fork.reveal: among walking's five blessings is that food and drink are well digested: a slow walk after a meal fits exactly.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: concentration, collectedness; the fifth blessing is samadhi that lasts.

trapdoor: what you thought: walking is good exercise.
what it means: walking practice supports the body, the effort of the path, and a steadiness that lasts into the day.
what a scholar hears: AN 5.29, the Cankama Sutta, lists the five benefits; the Pali texts often treat the body as the vehicle of practice rather than an obstacle.

sources.ref: AN 5.29, Cankama Sutta: the five benefits of walking meditation

121.title: Walking in the city
121.hook: the walk to the bus can be meditation too
121.howItsDone: Many Buddhist teachers encourage walking practice outside the retreat lane: on the way to work, in a parking lot, at a stoplight, simply knowing the body is walking while walking at a normal pace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the five blessings of walking: stamina, strength for effort, health, good digestion, and a concentration that lasts. Your line was walking steadies. Did you take a slow walk after a meal? Day one hundred twenty-one.

This week you've had a lane. Fifteen quiet steps, a slow turn, fifteen back. Lovely. Now picture Tuesday at 8:12. You're late, the coffee is too hot, the bus is two blocks away and pulling in. Nobody on that sidewalk is lifting, moving and placing. There's a horn, a dog, a man on a speakerphone. It's easy to think meditation lives in the lane and the city is where it goes to die. Today's question is simple: does the walk to the bus count too? The old texts have an answer, and it's a generous one.
screen: `FIFTEEN QUIET STEPS.` → `TUESDAY, 8:12, THE BUS.` → `DOES THIS WALK COUNT?`

segments.voice: The lane is a training ground, not the whole game. In the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness, the Buddha describes a practitioner who knows the body in every posture. When walking, they know they're walking. When standing, they know they're standing. Sitting, lying down: the same. The text then goes further. Going out and coming back, looking ahead and looking away, bending and stretching, eating, drinking, even using the toilet: all of it can be done with clear knowing. The word for that is sampajanna, clear comprehension. It means you know what you're doing while you're doing it, and why. Nothing in that list requires a quiet lane. So a city walk is a real practice, just a different one. In the lane you slow everything down. On the sidewalk you walk at a normal pace, eyes open, watching for traffic, because clear knowing includes knowing the curb is there. What you bring is the thread: the feel of the feet. Heel, sole, toes, the next foot. When the mind jumps to the meeting, the text message, the argument you're rehearsing, you notice it and come back to the feet. Some teachers use the city itself as the bell. Thich Nhat Hanh, the Vietnamese Zen teacher, suggested treating a red light or a ringing phone as a small call home to the breath. You're stopped anyway; you might as well arrive. So the walk to the bus isn't wasted time between practice sessions. For a lot of people with jobs and kids and commutes, it may be most of the practice they get. The feet are always with you.
screen: `THE LANE IS TRAINING, NOT THE GAME.` · `WALKING, KNOW YOU'RE WALKING.` · `NORMAL PACE, EYES OPEN, FEET FIRST.` · `A RED LIGHT AS A BELL.` · then, large: `EVERY STEP, HERE.`

segments.voice: Stand up if you can, wherever you are. Feel the floor under both feet. Now walk a few steps at your ordinary speed, the speed you'd walk to the bus, not the slow lane speed. Feel each foot land: heel, sole, toes. Stop. Stand. Let the breath come and go. Then sit, and for the rest of this time, picture tomorrow's first real walk: the door, the street, the corner. Pick one spot on that route, a crosswalk or a stoplight, that will be your bell. The bell holds the time.
Walking in the city. Knowing you're walking, at a normal pace, eyes open, with the feet as the thread and the street's own sounds as the bell.

Your line: every step, here. Today, on one real walk, even thirty seconds to the car or the mailbox, feel your feet the whole way. When you reach your chosen spot, arrive there. Day one hundred twenty-one.

what it means: every posture counts; walking to the bus, knowing you're walking, is practice.

122.title: Walking and sitting together
122.howItsDone: On most Buddhist meditation retreats the day alternates periods of sitting with periods of slow walking meditation, and many practitioners at home walk for a few minutes between sittings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, walking in the city: normal pace, eyes open, the feet as the thread. Your line was every step, here. Did a stoplight become a bell? Day one hundred twenty-two, the last day of the walking week.
screen: `WALKING IN THE CITY — EVERY STEP, HERE.`

segments.voice: Walk into almost any meditation retreat and look at the schedule taped to the wall. Sit. Walk. Sit. Walk. Sit. Lunch. Walk. Sit. It can look like somebody couldn't make up their mind. But ask anyone who has done a long retreat and they'll tell you: the walking isn't a break from the practice. After forty minutes on a cushion, the knees ache and the mind gets foggy. After forty minutes walking, the mind wants to settle down again. The two keep each other honest. Today, at the end of our walking week, we put them side by side.
screen: `SIT. WALK. SIT. WALK.` → `NOT A BREAK FROM PRACTICE.` → `THEY KEEP EACH OTHER HONEST.`

segments.voice: The pattern is old. In a discourse in the Numerical Discourses, the Buddha describes a monk who is devoted to wakefulness. By day, he says, the monk spends the time walking back and forth and sitting, clearing the mind of what gets in the way. In the first part of the night, the same: walking and sitting. In the middle of the night he lies down on his right side, like a resting lion, and sleeps, mindful of when to get up. In the last part of the night, walking and sitting again. Walking and sitting are named together, as one practice with two postures. Why pair them? Each covers the other's weak spot. Sitting is good for depth and stillness, but it can slide into sleepiness, which the texts call dullness, one of the five hindrances from last week. Walking wakes the body up and keeps you alert, but it can stay on the surface. So you sit until you start to fade, walk until you start to scatter, and sit again. Retreat teachers today still build the day that way. Look back at the week and you'll see what you've collected. The lane: twenty or thirty paces with nowhere to get to. Lifting, moving, placing. The turn that counts too. The five blessings, including concentration that lasts. And the sidewalk, where every step can be here. Put that beside the sitting you learned before, and you have two ways of doing the same thing: staying with this moment, whether the body is still or moving.
screen: `WALKING AND SITTING, NAMED TOGETHER.` · `SITTING GOES DEEP, BUT CAN FADE.` · `WALKING WAKES, BUT CAN SCATTER.` · `SIT, WALK, SIT: THE RETREAT DAY.` · then, large: `TWO WAYS TO STAY.`

segments.voice: If there's room, stand and walk slowly for about a minute. Ten steps, turn, ten steps back. Lift, move, place. At the turn, pause and feel the whole body standing. Then come back to your seat and sit, and let the stillness arrive in a body that has just been moving. Notice the difference: the feet quiet now, the breath taking over as the thread. Later today, if you have ten minutes, try the full version: sit five, walk five. The bell holds the time.
Walking and sitting together. Two postures, one practice: sit until you fade, walk until you scatter, and come back to stillness again.
Your line: two ways to stay. Today, when you've been sitting too long and the mind goes foggy, get up and walk a slow minute. When you're scattered, sit. Day one hundred twenty-two.

123.title: The three refuges
123.hook: the Buddha, the dhamma, the sangha: the three jewels people take refuge in
123.howItsDone: Buddhists recite the three refuges, usually three times in Pali or their own language, at the start of ceremonies, at home shrines and when formally becoming a lay follower.

segments.voice: Yesterday, walking and sitting together, the end of the walking week. Your line was two ways to stay. Did you get up and walk when the mind went foggy? Day one hundred twenty-three, and a new week: the refuges and the precepts.
screen: `WALKING AND SITTING — TWO WAYS TO STAY.`

segments.voice: Think about where you go when things fall apart. A person you call. A place, maybe a kitchen, a car, a bench. A habit: the phone, the fridge, the bed at four in the afternoon. Everybody has somewhere they run to. Some of those places actually hold you. Some just hide you for a while. Buddhism has a word for this, and a very old answer to the question of where to go. It's the first thing a person says when they become a Buddhist, and it's said at the start of almost every Buddhist ceremony on earth.
screen: `WHERE DO YOU RUN TO?` → `SOME PLACES HOLD YOU.` → `SOME JUST HIDE YOU.`

segments.voice: Tisarana. Ti: three. Sarana: shelter, a place of safety. The three refuges. They're also called the three jewels: the Buddha, the dhamma, the sangha. The Buddha is the one who woke up, and the proof that waking up is possible for a human being. The dhamma is what he taught, and the way things actually are. The sangha is the community that practices it: in the oldest sense the monks and nuns, and more broadly everyone walking the path. The Dhammapada knows the other kind of refuge well. In Max Muller's translation: "Men, driven by fear, go to many a refuge, to mountains and forests, to groves and sacred trees." The verses go on to say those refuges don't end suffering, and point to the three jewels instead. Here is the formula itself, in Pali, unchanged for well over two thousand years. Buddham saranam gacchami. Dhammam saranam gacchami. Sangham saranam gacchami. I go to the Buddha for refuge; to the dhamma; to the sangha. It's said three times, with the words for a second time and a third time in front. And there's a lovely detail in the early texts. The very first lay followers, two merchants named Tapussa and Bhallika, met the Buddha just after his awakening. They took refuge in only two jewels, because there was no sangha yet. The third refuge arrived when the community did. Notice what gacchami means: I go. Refuge isn't a place you sit inside. It's a direction you keep walking in. For many Buddhists, saying it is the beginning of each day's practice, not a one-time membership card.
screen: `TI-SARANA: THREE SHELTERS.` · `BUDDHA, DHAMMA, SANGHA.` · `THE FIRST TWO FOLLOWERS TOOK TWO.` · `GACCHAMI: I GO.` · then, large: `THREE PLACES TO REST.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. If you'd like to, and if it fits who you are, say the refuges quietly, the way Buddhists say them: Buddham saranam gacchami. Dhammam saranam gacchami. Sangham saranam gacchami. If you'd rather simply listen, let the three words land one at a time: someone woke up; there is a way; others walk it too. Then rest in the breath, as if you had arrived somewhere safe. The bell holds the time.
Tisarana. The three refuges: the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, the three jewels Buddhists go to for shelter.
Your line: three places to rest. Today, the next time you reach for a place to hide, the phone or the fridge, pause and ask whether it holds you or just hides you. Day one hundred twenty-three.

pairs: what he taught; the way things are

what it means: going, again and again, toward the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha.

124.title: Not killing
124.hook: precept one: I undertake the training to refrain from taking life
124.howItsDone: Buddhists recite the five precepts, often right after the three refuges, at temple visits and ceremonies; the first is to refrain from taking life, and many practice it by sparing insects and, in some traditions, by eating vegetarian food.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tisarana, the three refuges: the Buddha, the dhamma, the sangha. Your line was three places to rest. Did you notice where you went to hide? Day one hundred twenty-four.

There's a spider in the bathtub. You know the moment. The tissue is already in your hand. And then maybe you pause, and find a glass and a postcard, and walk it out to the garden like a tiny, ungrateful guest. Why pause? It's only a spider. Buddhists have been pausing like that for a very long time. After the refuges come five precepts, the basic ethics of a Buddhist life, and the first one is about exactly that moment. Today: precept one.
screen: `A SPIDER IN THE BATHTUB.` → `THE TISSUE, OR THE GLASS?` → `PRECEPT ONE.`

segments.voice: Here it is in Pali: Panatipata veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami. I undertake the training rule to refrain from taking life. Look at the shape of that sentence. It isn't a commandment handed down. It's a promise the person makes, in the first person, and the key word is sikkhapada: a training step. You're not claiming to be perfect. You're signing up to practice. Pana means breath, or a breathing thing. So the precept reaches past people to animals, down to the spider. The Dhammapada gives the reason in one line. In Max Muller's translation: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter." That's the whole argument: everything that lives wants to go on living, just like you. Another discourse puts it beautifully. It calls the five precepts great gifts. By not killing, you give every being around you freedom from fear, and you share in that safety yourself. Buddhists live this out in different ways, and it's fair to say so plainly. Many Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese monastics are vegetarian. In Theravada countries monks eat what they're given on the alms round, which can include meat, as long as the animal wasn't killed for them. Many lay Buddhists everywhere are vegetarian; many aren't. Where they agree is the core: don't take a life with your own intention. And the training starts small. The mosquito, the ant on the counter, the spider in the tub. Every one of them is a place to practice.
screen: `A TRAINING STEP, NOT A COMMANDMENT.` · `PANA: EVERYTHING THAT BREATHES.` · `ALL TREMBLE, ALL FEAR DEATH.` · `THE GIFT OF SAFETY.` · then, large: `LET IT LIVE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and feel the breath coming in and going out. That's pana, the breath of a living thing. Now think of the smallest creature you've seen today: a fly, an ant, a bird on a wire. Somewhere it's breathing too, in its own way, wanting to go on. Rest with that for a few breaths. Then make a simple plan: the next insect you meet today, you'll let it live, or carry it out. The bell holds the time.
Not killing. The first precept: a training, taken on freely, to refrain from taking the life of anything that breathes.
Your line: let it live. Today, let one insect live: a glass and a postcard, an open window, or just a pause before the swat. Day one hundred twenty-four.

pairs: freedom from fear for every being

each is a promise the person makes: 'I undertake the training rule.'
the first precept covers animals and insects, not only people
pana means anything that breathes.

many East Asian monastics are vegetarian; Theravada monks eat what they're given if it wasn't killed for them.

125.title: Not taking
125.hook: precept two: refrain from taking what is not given
125.howItsDone: Buddhists recite the second precept, to refrain from taking what is not given, along with the other four; monks and nuns go further and accept food and other things only when they are offered.

segments.voice: Yesterday, precept one, not killing: everything that breathes wants to go on. Your line was let it live. Did an insect get a glass and a postcard? Day one hundred twenty-five, precept two.

Quick inventory. Is there a book on your shelf that belongs to someone else? A casserole dish from a neighbor, a hoodie from an ex, a charger from work that somehow came home? Nobody here is a burglar. But most of us are holding onto something that was never quite given. The second precept doesn't sound like it's about you. It sounds like it's about thieves. Listen to how it's actually worded, though, and it gets much closer to home.
screen: `A BORROWED BOOK. A NEIGHBOR'S DISH.` → `NOBODY HERE IS A BURGLAR.` → `PRECEPT TWO.`

segments.voice: In Pali: Adinnadana veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami. I undertake the training rule to refrain from taking what is not given. Adinna: not given. Adana: taking. Notice it doesn't say don't steal. It says don't take what isn't given. That's a wider door. Stealing is only the loud version. The quiet versions are everywhere: the book you meant to return, the extra change the cashier handed you by mistake, the credit for a colleague's idea, the hour of someone's time you took without asking. In each case, the question is the same. Was this freely handed to me, or did I just take it? The early discourses describe a person who keeps this precept as someone who doesn't take, in the village or in the forest, what belongs to someone else. And the rule for monks and nuns is even stricter: they may not take anything at all, not even food, unless it's offered. A monk won't pick an apple off a table until someone hands it to him. That's why, next week, you'll meet the alms round. The flip side of not taking is generosity, which is where this whole path of practice is heading. A person trained in only what's given lives with a certain lightness. Nobody's looking for them. Nothing in the house is a small, guilty weight. And there's a strange kind of freedom in that: what you have, you really have, because it was given. Teachers today often widen the precept further, to time, to attention, to credit. The old wording holds all of it: only what's given.
screen: `ADINNA: NOT GIVEN. ADANA: TAKING.` · `WIDER THAN STEALING.` · `MONKS TAKE NOTHING UNOFFERED.` · `WHAT YOU HAVE, YOU REALLY HAVE.` · then, large: `ONLY WHAT'S GIVEN.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Now take a slow walk, in your mind, through your home. The shelves. The kitchen. The closet. The desk drawer. Is there anything there that was lent to you and never gone home? Don't judge it; just notice it, and notice how it feels to find it. If something comes to mind, picture yourself handing it back, and the other person's face. Then return to the breath, which nobody lent you. The bell holds the time.
Not taking. The second precept: a training to take only what is freely given, which reaches much further than stealing.
Your line: only what's given. Today, return one thing you borrowed, or send a text to set it up: the book, the dish, the charger. Day one hundred twenty-five.

pairs: won't take it until it's offered

it's wider: refrain from taking what is not given.
monks and nuns won't even take food unless it's offered
the monastic rule is stricter than the lay precept.
the precept only matters for valuable things
the quiet versions count too: the borrowed book, the extra change, the credit.

options: keep it: you didn't take it, they gave it.
fork.reveal: it wasn't really given, only given by mistake. the precept's question is whether it was freely handed to you.

original.note: Pali: taking what is not given (adinna, not given + adana, taking).

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule for thieves.
what it means: a training to take only what is freely given, including time and credit.
what a scholar hears: adinnadana, literally 'not-given-taking'; the monastic code treats it as grave enough that a serious theft ends a monk's ordination.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 41 (Saleyyaka Sutta), abstaining from taking what is not given
Vinaya, Parajika 2 (taking what is not given)

126.title: Sexual conduct
126.hook: precept three: refrain from sexual misconduct; harm, not shame, is the measure
126.howItsDone: Lay Buddhists recite the third precept with the other four; communities interpret its details differently, and monks and nuns keep full celibacy under their monastic rule.

segments.voice: Yesterday, precept two, not taking: the borrowed book, the extra change. Your line was only what's given. Did anything go back where it belonged? Day one hundred twenty-six, precept three.

Some people brace a little when religion gets to this subject. They're expecting a list of forbidden things and a raised eyebrow. They've heard sex talked about as dirty, or dangerous, or something to be ashamed of. The third precept surprises a lot of people, because shame isn't its measure. It asks a different question, the same one the first two precepts asked about life and about things: is anyone being harmed? Today, precept three, told plainly.
screen: `BRACING FOR THE LIST.` → `NOT SHAME.` → `IS ANYONE HARMED?`

segments.voice: In Pali: Kamesu micchacara veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami. I undertake the training rule to refrain from misconduct in sensual pleasures. Kama means sensual pleasure, desire. Micchacara means wrong conduct, literally going the wrong way. What the precept names isn't desire itself. Lay Buddhists marry, fall in love, raise families, and the texts treat that as a normal human life. What it names is going the wrong way with desire. The early discourses make that concrete. They describe someone who keeps this precept as not getting involved with people who are under someone else's protection, or who are promised to someone else. In the world those texts came from, that meant a daughter in her family's care, or a wife or a betrothed woman. The thread running through the list is harm: to the other person, to a partner who trusted you, to families. That's why teachers today often put it in a single line: harm, not shame, is the measure. Honesty, consent, keeping the promises you've made, not using another person. Buddhist communities read the details in different ways, and it's fair to say so plainly. More traditional communities keep closely to the old lists. Many teachers, especially in newer communities, focus on the principle of not causing harm and apply it to every kind of relationship. Monks and nuns go further still: they keep complete celibacy. What they all share is the heart of it. Desire is human. What you do with it can heal or wound. The precept is a training in the first.

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone close to you: a partner, a friend, a parent, a child. Think of one promise you've made them, big or small. I'll be home by six. I'll call you back. I'll be honest with you. Hold that promise gently, the way you'd hold something that belongs to both of you. Notice the trust inside it. Then, if you like, send them the old wish from the metta weeks: may you be safe, may you be at ease. The bell holds the time.
Sexual conduct. The third precept: a training not to go the wrong way with desire, where the measure is harm, not shame.
Your line: no harm in love. Today, keep one promise to someone close, exactly as you made it: on time, in full, without being reminded. Day one hundred twenty-six.
